scope: src/levelSequences.js (full file, 3831 lines) — level scripting/sequence data + element builders + runtime entry (applySequenceLayout). Cross-referenced against src/main.js wiring: applySequenceLayout call (main.js:5288), _shatterMesh (main.js:33210), coverHP degradation (main.js:26513), fakeCeilingLamps lighting controller (main.js:2262-2351, flicker tick 44110), _aaPhysicalGlass (main.js:2433), vault list consumption (main.js:27885+).

findings.title: crate2: shooting the TOP crate destroys the BOTTOM crate (linkedSibling semantics inverted vs _shatterMesh)
findings.description: The two-box crate stack sets `b.userData.linkedSibling = a` on the TOP crate, with the comment '// top breaks -> bottom still cover'. But the runtime's _shatterMesh treats linkedSibling as a mesh to DELETE when the holder breaks (main.js:33228-33229: scene.remove(sib); sib.geometry.dispose(); sib.material.dispose()). That hook exists for the `window` builder, where the pane's linkedSibling is its decorative highlight strip. So when the player shoots the top crate to break it, _shatterMesh(b) removes and disposes `a` — the bottom crate — doing the exact opposite of the comment: the lower cover vanishes. crate2 is used in B1 BE, B4 BE, B5 BW, B6 MW, B7 (3x), B9, B10, B11, B12, so this is visible in most levels.
findings.evidence: b.userData.linkedSibling = a;  // top breaks -> bottom still cover  // …but _shatterMesh: const sib=mesh.userData.linkedSibling; if(sib){scene.remove(sib);if(sib.geometry)sib.geometry.dispose();if(sib.material&&sib.material.dispose)sib.material.dispose();}
findings.fix: Remove the `b.userData.linkedSibling = a;` line (line 1380). linkedSibling is a 'remove this decorative child' hook, not a 'keep this as cover' link; the two crates should break independently. Each box already has its own coverHP. Optionally also store `a.userData.linkedTop = b` only if you intend to make bottom-break drop the top — but do NOT reuse linkedSibling for it.
findings.risk: Removing the line cannot break anything that currently works (the current behavior is wrong). No save-compat or perf concern; the geometry is rebuilt per level. Leaves the top crate floating if the bottom breaks first (see crate2-bottom-break-floating), which is a separate, pre-existing issue.

findings.title: crate2: bottom crate's wall/vault AABB removed on break leaves the top crate floating; top break leaves bottom's collider orphaned
findings.description: Only the BOTTOM box `a` owns linkedAABB/linkedVault (lines 1374-1375). When `a` breaks, _shatterMesh marks aabb.broken/vlEntry.broken so movement/AI/vault clear — but the TOP box `b` is never removed and is not linked to anything, so it floats in mid-air with no collider. Conversely the TOP box `b` has NO linkedAABB/linkedVault, so when `b` is destroyed (and, per the inverted-sibling bug, it also deletes `a`), the wall AABB and vault entry created for `a` are never marked broken — leaving an invisible solid collider + phantom vault prompt where both visible meshes are gone.
findings.evidence: a.userData.linkedAABB = aabb; a.userData.linkedVault = vaultE;  (only on bottom box `a`)  …  const b = new THREE.Mesh(...); b.position.set(e.x + 0.1, WT + h*1.45, e.z - 0.05); … (no linkedAABB/linkedVault on `b`)
findings.fix: Give each box its own AABB/vault entry: build a separate `aabbTop`/`vaultTop` for `b` and set b.userData.linkedAABB/linkedVault to them. Since the bottom is the only piece at floor/chest height, the simplest correct fix is to only register colliders for `a` AND make `b` non-blocking decoration (mark b.userData.noBlock) so it never needs its own collider — then the floating-top concern is purely visual. Pair this with removing the inverted linkedSibling.
findings.risk: Adding a second AABB slightly increases wl/vl length (negligible). Changing b to noBlock would let players/AI clip the upper crate corner — acceptable since it sits above chest height. Keep nav-grid bake in mind; entries are processed in the same pass.

findings.title: EXTRA_ELEMENTS[1] and ROUTE_COMPLETION_ELEMENTS_BY_BN[1] are never executed (B01 returns early)
findings.description: applySequenceLayout returns immediately after applyB01DesignedDockLevel(ctx) for bn===1 (line 62-65), BEFORE the loops that consume EXTRA_ELEMENTS[bn] (lines 99-103) and ROUTE_COMPLETION_ELEMENTS_BY_BN[bn] (lines 108-112). Yet EXTRA_ELEMENTS[1] (lines 3480-3547, ~37 elements) and ROUTE_COMPLETION_ELEMENTS_BY_BN[1] (lines 3393-3398, 4 kits) are fully authored. They are dead code. Worse, they reuse the SAME geometryIds as the hand-authored dock (e.g. 'west_service_run', 'dock_threshold_strip', 'relay_partition_north', 'relay_partition_west', 'relay_offset_door', 'manifest_office_window', 'east_compression_corridor', 'foreman_cage_wall', 'foreman_glass', 'catwalk_to_cage_window', 'intake_apron_divider', 'mid_spine_pinch', 'cage_vestibule', 'relay_side_slit', 'alarm_interact_lane'), so if anyone moved the early-return or special-cased B01 differently the level would get duplicated/competing geometry with conflicting ids.
findings.evidence: if (bn === 1) { applyB01DesignedDockLevel(ctx); return; }  …  const extras = EXTRA_ELEMENTS[bn] || []; (never reached for bn===1)
findings.fix: Delete EXTRA_ELEMENTS[1] (lines 3480-3547) and ROUTE_COMPLETION_ELEMENTS_BY_BN[1] (lines 3393-3398) since they are superseded by applyB01DesignedDockLevel, OR add a comment at the early return making clear B01 intentionally skips both tables. If removing, double-check no tooling/audit script enumerates EXTRA_ELEMENTS[1] (grep scripts/*.mjs).
findings.risk: Pure dead-code removal; no runtime behavior change for B01 today. Risk only if an external audit script reads these arrays — verify before deleting; otherwise keep but annotate.

findings.title: Primary tactical-glass `window` builder uses flat MeshPhongMaterial while ctx.aaPhysicalGlass (transmission glass) sits unused
findings.description: The `window` builder is the dominant glass element across all 11 procedural buildings (every EXTRA_ELEMENTS list and serviceHall/glassPreview/vestibuleThreshold kits funnel through it). It hard-codes a plain MeshPhongMaterial with opacity 0.22 and no transmission/refraction. Meanwhile ctx.aaPhysicalGlass (the real MeshPhysicalMaterial with transmission/IOR, used by the rarely-instanced `glass` builder at line 1152 and the B01-only addB01Glass at line 333) is available in ctx but never used here. The result: almost all in-game windows read as a flat tinted plane, while the few `glass` partitions look like real glass — an inconsistency the player sees immediately on every level.
findings.evidence: const glassM = new THREE.MeshPhongMaterial({ color: e.col || 0xa8c8e0, transparent: true, opacity: 0.22, shininess: 220, specular: 0xffffff, depthWrite: false });  // ctx.aaPhysicalGlass available but not called
findings.fix: Mirror the `glass` builder's quality gate: at line 1653, if (ctx.settings?.quality === 'high' || 'ultra') && typeof ctx.aaPhysicalGlass === 'function', build glassM = ctx.aaPhysicalGlass({color:e.col||0xa8c8e0, shininess:220, specular:0xffffff, transparent:true, opacity:0.22}, {transmission:0.42, thickness:0.06, roughness:0.12}); else fall back to the existing phong. Keep userData.glassPane=true so the solids filter still includes it (transmission materials are transparent and would otherwise be excluded — main.js:37925 keeps glassPane in solids).
findings.risk: MeshPhysicalMaterial/transmission is more expensive; gate behind quality like the `glass` builder already does. Verify breakability still works: pane keeps glassPane/breakable userData so _shatterMesh path is unaffected. No save-compat impact.

findings.title: def.lights `flicker` flag (and pend `flicker`) is stored but never animated — fakeCeilingLamps don't flicker
findings.description: Per-building accent lights set userData {flicker:true, flickerPhase:…} when L.flicker is truthy (line 121) and push them through pushFakeAccent into fakeCeilingLamps. But the lighting controller (main.js:2309-2351) only reads F.position and F.color from fakeCeilingLamps for nearest-lamp chroma; it never reads flicker/flickerPhase/baseIntensity to modulate intensity. The actual flicker tick (main.js:44110-44114) operates on real THREE PointLights' .intensity, which fake lamps don't have. So the `flicker:true` entries in many def.lights (B1, B5, B6, B9, B10, B12) and `flicker` on pend lights produce no visible flicker from these accents.
findings.evidence: const flick = L.flicker ? { flicker: true, flickerPhase: Math.random() * 10, sequenceDefLight: true } : { sequenceDefLight: true }; pushFakeAccent(ctx, x, y, z, col, baseIntensity, flick);  // flicker userData never consumed for fake lamps
findings.fix: Either (a) drop the flicker plumbing from def.lights/pend to avoid implying an effect that doesn't fire, or (b) wire the lighting controller's tick to modulate the nearest fake lamp's effective intensity using F.userData.flicker/flickerPhase (add a small noise term to lampNear or pool intensity when the nearest fake lamp flickers). Option (b) is the AAA-positive choice for the medical/dock/subway 'failing fluorescent' mood.
findings.risk: Option (b) touches the per-frame lighting tick (hot path) — keep it cheap (single sin/noise on the already-selected nearest lamp). Option (a) is zero-risk cleanup. Real ceiling PointLights still flicker, so current mood is only partially lost.

findings.title: bench backrest placed at un-rotated -z offset, so rotated benches (rotY=π/2) have a detached/misplaced backrest
findings.description: In `bench`, the seat mesh is positioned at (e.x,e.z) and rotated by e.rotY correctly. The backrest `bk` is positioned at bx=e.x, bz=e.z - d*0.5 + 0.05 (an offset along WORLD -z) and only THEN rotated in place (bk.rotation.y=e.rotY). For benches with rotY=π/2 the backrest should sit along the rotated -d axis (world -x), not world -z. Many benches use rotY:Math.PI/2 with back:true (lines 2237, 2247, 2430, 2431, 2675, 2713, 3146, 3147), so their backrests end up offset 90° from the seat and clip into adjacent space.
findings.evidence: const bx = e.x, bz = e.z - d*0.5 + 0.05; bk.position.set(bx, WT + h + 0.35, bz); if (e.rotY) { bk.rotation.y = e.rotY; }
findings.fix: Rotate the local backrest offset by e.rotY before applying: const c=Math.cos(e.rotY||0), s=Math.sin(e.rotY||0); const off=-d*0.5+0.05; bk.position.set(e.x + s*off, WT+h+0.35, e.z + c*off); bk.rotation.y = e.rotY||0; (matches the offset convention used elsewhere, e.g. tall stripes at line 676-678).
findings.risk: Cosmetic prop placement only; no collider involvement (backrest is decoration, not pushed to wl). Low risk. Verify the rotY=0 benches still look identical (s=0,c=1 reduces to current offset).

findings.title: bed headboard offset not rotated (latent — all current beds use rotY:0)
findings.description: Same class of bug as the bench backrest: the headboard is positioned at e.z + d*0.5 - 0.20 (world +z) then rotated in place. If a bed is authored with a non-zero rotY the headboard will detach from the bed. Currently all `bed` entries (B5 FE/MW) pass rotY:0, so this is latent, not active — flagged for consistency/future-proofing alongside the bench fix.
findings.evidence: head.position.set(e.x, WT + h + 0.20, e.z + d*0.5 - 0.20); if (e.rotY) { head.rotation.y = e.rotY; }
findings.fix: Rotate the +d/2 head offset by e.rotY like the bench fix: const c=Math.cos(e.rotY||0), s=Math.sin(e.rotY||0); const off=d*0.5-0.20; head.position.set(e.x - s*off, WT+h+0.20, e.z + c*off); head.rotation.y=e.rotY||0; (apply the same to base/top if you ever want a rotated bed — those use full BoxGeometry so they rotate correctly already).
findings.risk: Latent only; zero behavioral change for existing rotY:0 beds. Trivial.

findings.title: desk L-shape: second bar hard-codes rotY:0 and uses world-axis lx/lz offsets, so a rotated desk would break (latent)
findings.description: `desk` builds an L from two `bar` calls. The first bar inherits e.rotY (via {...e}); the second bar hard-codes rotY:0 and offsets by world-space e.lx/e.lz. If a desk were authored with rotY != 0 the L would split apart (first arm rotated, second arm not). No desk in the data passes rotY today, so latent. Also worth noting the first bar spreads `...e` which carries e.t:'desk' and any stray fields into `bar` (harmless).
findings.evidence: ELEMENT_BUILDERS.bar(ctx, { ...e, x: e.x + (e.lx || 1.55), z: e.z + (e.lz || 1.20), w: 0.7, d: 1.8, h: 1.05, rotY: 0, top: 0xc8a040, glow: e.glow });
findings.fix: If desks should support rotation: rotate the (lx,lz) offset by e.rotY and pass rotY:e.rotY to the second bar. If desks are intentionally axis-aligned forever, leave a comment noting rotY is unsupported. Low priority since unused.
findings.risk: Latent; no current desk uses rotY. Zero risk to leave as-is.

findings.title: arch rotY rotates each piece about its own center, not the arch center (latent — no arch passes rotY)
findings.description: When e.rotY is set, the arch builder does [post1,post2,lin,ac].forEach(p => p.rotation.y = e.rotY) but the posts were positioned at e.x±w/2 in world space. Rotating each piece about its own local origin (not the arch's center) leaves the posts at the same XZ while spinning them, producing a broken arch. The inline comment even acknowledges 'Rotate whole arch as a group: simpler — re-rotate each piece.' All arch entries pass no rotY today, so latent.
findings.evidence: if (e.rotY) { [post1, post2, lin, ac].forEach(p => p.rotation.y = e.rotY); }
findings.fix: To support rotation, recompute each piece's position by rotating its local offset (±w/2, etc.) about (e.x,e.z) by e.rotY, then set rotation.y. Or wrap the four meshes in a THREE.Group placed at (e.x,WT,e.z), add children at local offsets, and rotate the group. Low priority (unused).
findings.risk: Latent; zero risk if left unchanged.

findings.title: Element builders `spine`, `offsetRoom`, and `containerrow` are defined but never referenced
findings.description: ELEMENT_BUILDERS.spine (line 1538), ELEMENT_BUILDERS.offsetRoom (line 1957), and ELEMENT_BUILDERS.containerrow (line 1588) are never used by any SEQUENCE_DEFS / EXTRA_ELEMENTS / ROUTE_COMPLETION table (verified by enumerating all `t:'…'` values vs defined builders). `gate` is used internally by `turnstiles`, so it is NOT dead. These three are harmless library functions but are pure dead weight in the bundle.
findings.evidence: DEFINED-but-unused builders: containerrow, offsetRoom, spine (gate is used by turnstiles, so excluded).
findings.fix: Either remove them, or keep them as an authoring kit and add a brief '// authoring kit (currently unreferenced)' comment so a future cleanup pass doesn't mistake them for live code. No urgency.
findings.risk: Removal is safe (no references). Keeping them costs only a few KB. No save-compat/perf concern.

findings.title: forklift collider AABB uses hard-coded depth 2.0 vs body depth 1.9, and ignores the forks that protrude +1.2 in z
findings.description: The forklift body BoxGeometry is 1.4(w) x 1.05(h) x 1.9(d), but the wall AABB uses Math.abs(...)*1.4/2 and *2.0/2 (depth 2.0, not 1.9). Minor over-size on depth. More noticeably, the fork tines mesh is placed at e.z + 1.2 (0.45 beyond the AABB half-depth of ~1.0), so the visible forks stick out past the collider — bullets/players pass through the forks. Cosmetic/collision mismatch; forklifts are sparse (B1 FW/FE, B9 FE).
findings.evidence: const ax = Math.abs(c)*1.4/2 + Math.abs(s)*2.0/2; const az = Math.abs(s)*1.4/2 + Math.abs(c)*2.0/2;  // body d is 1.9; fork at e.z+1.2 lies outside AABB
findings.fix: Use the real body depth (1.9) and extend the AABB forward to cover the forks, e.g. base footprint on a 1.4 x ~2.6 envelope offset toward +z, or add a second small AABB for the fork tines. Low priority.
findings.risk: Slightly enlarging the forklift collider could marginally tighten nearby pathing; keep the change small. Cosmetic otherwise.
